conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you could come in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I know these first weeks with a baby can feel like riding a wave of joy, exhaustion, and everything in-between, so we routinely check in on how moms are coping.

Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally during the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s simply a way for us to make sure we’re giving you the right support. Everything you share is confidential, and you can take your time or pause at any point. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question.

*settles into the chair, adjusting the diaper bag beside me and brushing a stray piece of hair back*  
Okay… thank you. I guess I’m ready. I’ve just been so tired lately, but if this can help figure out what’s going on, I’m willing to try.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*gives a small shrug, eyes on the blanket peeking out of the diaper bag*  
Sometimes I still laugh—like when my sister sent that silly video—but mostly it feels kind of forced. Things that used to crack me up just feel… flat. I guess I do laugh, just not as easily as before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shifts in the chair, folding and unfolding the edge of a burp cloth*  
I still look forward to little stuff—like when my husband gets home so I’m not alone with the baby, or that first quiet cup of coffee—but the big things I used to plan feel kind of… heavy. Like I’ll think, “It’d be nice to go to brunch,” but then I picture packing the diaper bag, the car seat, worrying she’ll cry the whole time, and the excitement just drains out. So yeah, I still have moments of “can’t wait,” just not as many and not as strong.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*quiet for a moment, eyes fixed on my lap*  
Sometimes… like last night, she wouldn’t settle for two hours, and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I didn’t swaddle her tight enough. My husband said it’s just what babies do, but I still felt like I must’ve missed something. It’s not all the time, but yeah, when she’s fussy or won’t sleep, my mind jumps to what I might’ve done wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*twists the burp cloth tighter in my hands*  
Yeah... like yesterday she took a super-long nap—almost four hours—and instead of resting I kept creeping in to make sure she was still breathing. My heart would race every time I couldn't see her chest moving right away. And sometimes, when she's just quietly staring at me, this wave of dread hits that maybe I'm already messing her up somehow. I know it doesn't make sense, but the worry just shows up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifts restlessly in the chair*  
Now and then. A couple nights ago I was feeding her in the dark and suddenly felt like the walls were closing in—heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. Nothing had changed; she was quiet, my husband was asleep down the hall, but for a minute I thought I might pass out. It passed after a few seconds, but it left me shaky. It’s only happened a few times this week, and I can’t point to any real reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, exhaling*  
Yeah… most days I feel like I’m treading water. I’ll finish one feeding and realize there’s laundry piled up, the trash needs to go out, I haven’t eaten, and she’s already rooting to eat again. I keep making little lists, but they just get longer. I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I can never quite catch up, and the thought of tomorrow feels tiring before I’ve even closed my eyes tonight.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*runs a hand across tired eyes*  
I wouldn’t say I’m up all night crying or anything, but once she finally goes down, my brain keeps spinning—did I sterilize the pump parts, is she gaining enough weight, will she wake up in thirty minutes again? I lie there staring at the ceiling or scrolling my phone, and before I know it an hour’s gone. It’s happened maybe four nights this week, and then of course she wakes for a feed just when I’ve drifted off. So yeah, getting to sleep’s been rough.
I have felt sad or miserable

*glances down at the baby blanket in my lap*  
I do feel sad some of the time—not every minute, but it sneaks up. Like yesterday, while folding her tiny onesies, I just started tearing up thinking, “I should be enjoying this more.” It’s not a constant dark cloud, more like little showers that come and go. I’d say I’ve felt pretty miserable maybe three or four days out of the last week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shakes head quickly*  
No, I haven’t actually cried—at least not real tears. My eyes have welled up a couple times, like when the pediatrician said she’s a little slow gaining weight, but I always manage to blink it away before it spills over. So, no actual crying fits this week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks up quickly, eyes wide*  
No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family. I might feel overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind, not even for a second.

I hear how hard you're working to care for your baby while feeling like the joy is slipping through your fingers. You shared that laughter feels <quote>forced</quote>, that simple outings now seem exhausting, and that waves of dread or sudden panic catch you off guard. Despite these heavy feelings, you're still showing up-feeding, soothing, checking on her breathing-demonstrating deep love and protectiveness.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is now "forced" and things feel "flat," indicating a clear reduction in ability to enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient still anticipates small daily pleasures but reports diminished enthusiasm and avoidance of bigger activities, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>The mother acknowledges self-blame "sometimes" when the baby is fussy, matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intrusive worries about infant safety and parenting competence that are disproportionate and persistent, indicating anxiety "very often."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes occurring multiple times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent daily overwhelm and chronic fatigue but is still managing basic tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes repeated difficulty initiating sleep 4 nights this week due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad/miserable on 3–4 of the past 7 days, which aligns with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 17 (≥14) places the patient above the cutoff for <med>probable peripartum depression</med>. She endorses core symptoms: persistent low mood, loss of interest (<sym>things feel flat</sym>), fatigue, guilt, and multiple anxiety features meeting <med>DSM-5</med> threshold for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset. Q10 score 0 indicates no current self-harm thoughts, but high anxiety scores warrant immediate support. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>obstetric provider</med> within one week
2. Discuss <med>SSRIs</med> or other evidence-based treatments safe for breastfeeding
3. Begin weekly cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy focused on postpartum issues
4. Encourage 20-30 minutes of gentle outdoor activity daily to boost mood
5. Plan partner or family member to take one night feeding to protect <sym>sleep</sym>
6. Introduce <med>postpartum support groups</med> for shared experience and normalization
7. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first child, breastfeeding. Partner supportive, no prior psych history per brief chart review.

Presenting concerns endorsed during EPDS-style interview:

- Mood: “Sad or miserable” 3–4 days past week; anhedonia (“things feel flat,” “excitement drains out”); no tearful episodes but eyes “welled up.”  
- Anxiety: Excessive worry about infant safety (checking breathing), intrusive dread of “messing her up,” 2–3 brief nocturnal panic attacks (“heart pounding, walls closing in”).  
- Cognitions: Self-blame when baby fussy; guilt over “not enjoying this more.”  
- Functioning: Sleep onset delay 4/7 nights (racing thoughts, not infant-related); daily tasks “never caught up,” anticipatory fatigue.

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation; protective of infant.

Screening significance  
Elevated scores consistent with possible postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Meets threshold items: low mood, loss of enjoyment, guilt, anxiety/panic, sleep disruption, feeling overwhelmed. No suicidal ideation.

Recommendation: Continue monitoring with formal EPDS scoring, consider referral for perinatal mental health assessment and support resources.
